I've been working this land since I was young. Twelve mu isn't much but it feeds my family and earns enough cash to get by. My wheat and maize rotation I could do with my eyes closed at this point. Cotton is harder work every year but I keep a few mu because in a good year it pays better than grain.

**My thinking for this year:**

My 8 mu of flat ground runs wheat in winter and maize in summer — same fields, back to back. That's how we've always done it here in Quzhou. I'll plant wheat in October after maize comes off. I always plow first to bury the stubble and then put down compound fertilizer before seeding. I use the improved variety I get from the county seed store — same one my neighbors use, and it's never let me down. Come spring I'll run the well pump at jointing stage and again near heading. Two sprays: one for weeds in early spring, one for disease control around flowering. I expect around 450 jin per mu, which is normal for my land.

For summer maize, I plant right after wheat harvest — no delay, not even a day if I can help it. I use hybrid seed, the same kind I've been buying the last eight or nine years. Good yields, strong stalks. I plant into the stubble directly — no need to plow again in summer, and it saves time. I'll put down some base fertilizer at planting and top-dress at the big bell stage. The rain usually covers July and August but if it gets dry I'll irrigate once from the well. A couple of sprays — one for weeds early and one for borers later.

My 4 mu of cotton I prep in April with the rotary tiller. I use Bt hybrid seed now — less bollworm spraying than the old days, which is good because I'm not as fast moving around the field anymore at 60. Still need to watch for aphids and spider mites. Cotton needs water at several stages so I'll irrigate four times from the well. Cotton takes more out of the soil so I put down more potassium than with grain.
